title: Characterizing supersolid phase transitions in trapped quantum gases with tilted dipoles at finite temperature
authors: Julian Kusch, Lauriane Chomaz, Wyatt Kirkby
abstract: Motivated by a recent experimental work arXiv:2608.20327, we theoretically investigate the nature of phase transitions in a trapped dipolar quantum gas upon tuning the contact interaction strength and dipole orientation. Using extended Gross-Pitaevskii simulations including thermal and quantum effects, we map the phase diagram comprising unmodulated superfluids, triangular droplet arrays, and stripe states. We further characterize the order of the transitions separating them through imaginary-time hysteresis analysis. The unmodulated-to-modulated transition evolves from discontinuous to continuous with increasing dipole tilt before becoming discontinuous again at large tilts. The degree of continuity is further affected by particle number, temperature, and confinement. While continuous behavior generally correlates with the emergence of stripe states, this correspondence is not systematic, and finite-size effects also influence the continuity of the transition. The triangular-to-stripe transition is found to be discontinuous at small contact interaction strengths and becomes increasingly continuous upon approaching the unmodulated-to-modulated phase boundary. Our results reveal a tunable transition order in finite dipolar quantum gases and provide guidance for its experimental investigation.
summary: This theoretical study characterizes the phase transitions within trapped dipolar quantum gases by simulating the system using an extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation. The authors use imaginary-time hysteresis analysis to map out how the transition order—whether continuous or discontinuous—can be tuned by adjusting the dipole tilt angle and interaction strengths. The findings provide crucial guidance for future experimental measurements in dipolar quantum gases.
main_problem: The paper investigates the nature and tunability of phase transitions (e.g., unmodulated-to-modulated, triangular-to-stripe) in trapped dipolar quantum gases at finite temperature.
main_result: The transition order is found to be tunable by parameters like dipole tilt angle and contact interaction strength, exhibiting transitions between continuous and discontinuous regimes.
method: The study employs extended Gross-Pitaevskii simulations incorporating both thermal and quantum fluctuation effects, using imaginary-time hysteresis analysis to determine transition order.
model_or_system: The system is a trapped dipolar quantum gas, modeled using an extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation that includes terms for harmonic trapping, contact interactions, dipolar interactions, and both thermal and quantum fluctuations.
key_observables: Phase diagram mapping (unmodulated, triangular, stripe states), transition order (discontinuous vs. continuous), and density modulation contrast.
important_parameters: Dipole tilt angle ($\alpha$), contact interaction strength ($a_s$), temperature ($T$), particle number ($N$), and the relative dipolar interaction strength ($\epsilon_{	ext{dd}}$).
main_assumptions: The treatment of quantum fluctuations relies on a local-density approximation, and the thermal fluctuation term uses an ansatz approximation rather than a momentum cutoff.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the system geometry in a surfboard-shaped trap, show the thermal fluctuation energy dependence on density, and display density contrast curves used for hysteresis analysis across different dipole tilt angles.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using the extended GPE, then maps the phase diagram by analyzing the transition order using hysteresis analysis, and finally discusses the structural classification of the resulting supersolid phases (triangular vs. stripe) using momentum-space diagnostics.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the complex interplay between dipolar interactions, thermal fluctuations, and quantum correlations in ultracold atomic systems, providing quantitative predictions for experimentally observable phase transitions.
